Async behavior::Async UI.summary: Wait for asynchronous UI changes with awaited findBy queries and waitFor assertions. Use findBy when content should appear; use waitFor when an assertion must eventually pass.
Async behavior::Async UI.explanation: Async queries return promises and should be awaited. Use findBy when an element is expected to appear after a delayed UI change; use waitFor when an existing assertion must become true over time. The retry continues until the callback stops throwing or the timeout is reached.
Async behavior::Async UI.syntax: function waitFor<T>(callback: () => T | Promise<T>, options?: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }): Promise<T>

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: The callback that returns a value or promise; waitFor retries it until it stops throwing.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }
parameters.description: Optional container, timeout, interval, onTimeout, and mutation-observer settings.

Async behavior::Async UI.returns: A Promise resolving to the callback result.

A findBy call can receive waitFor configuration after its query arguments.
Choose findBy for delayed loading, success, or error content that eventually appears in the DOM.
Use waitFor to retry an assertion rather than inserting a fixed sleep into the test.

Use waitForElementToBeRemoved when testing that a loading or other transient element disappears.
gotchas: Always await findBy and waitFor calls; otherwise the test can finish before the asynchronous assertion completes.
Keep the waitFor callback focused and make its assertion throw while the expected condition is not yet true.
An async waitFor callback is not retried until its returned promise rejects, so structure asynchronous callbacks deliberately.

Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.summary: Use findBy queries to await an element that should appear asynchronously. Use waitFor to retry an assertion or callback until it succeeds or times out.
Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.explanation: findBy queries combine a getBy query with waitFor and return a promise that resolves when the matching element appears. Use waitFor to repeatedly run an assertion until it stops throwing or the timeout is reached; await either utility because both are asynchronous.
Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.syntax: function waitFor<T>(callback: () => T | Promise<T>, options?: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }): Promise<T>

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Callback returning a value or promise; it is retried while it throws.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: {container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit}
parameters.description: Optional container, timeout, interval, timeout handler, and mutation observer settings.

Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.returns: waitFor returns a Promise<T>; findBy returns a Promise resolving to the matching element and rejects when no unique match is found within the timeout.

Pass query arguments first and waitFor configuration last when customizing findBy.
Use findBy for eventual appearance rather than an element that must already exist.
Use waitFor when the condition is an assertion or other callback result, not simply locating one element.
waitFor retries a throwing callback until it succeeds or the configured timeout expires.

Async behavior::MSW and network boundari.summary: Use MSW to mock HTTP at the network boundary while the component performs its real request. This lets tests verify realistic success and server-error UI states with async, user-facing queries.
Async behavior::MSW and network boundari.explanation: MSW intercepts the HTTP request at the server boundary, allowing the component to run its normal fetch logic. The test supplies a declarative handler, starts the mock server for the suite, resets handlers between tests, and closes it afterward; async queries then wait for the resulting UI.

example.title: Test a successful request
example.code:
import {http, HttpResponse} from 'msw'
import {setupServer} from 'msw/node'
import {render, fireEvent, screen} from '@testing-library/react'
import '@testing-library/jest-dom'
import Fetch from './Fetch'

const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/greeting', () =>
    HttpResponse.json({greeting: 'hello there'}),
  ),
)

beforeAll(() => server.listen())
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())
afterAll(() => server.close())

test('loads and displays greeting', async () => {
  render(<Fetch url="/greeting" />)
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Load Greeting'))
  expect(await screen.findByRole('heading')).toHaveTextContent('hello there')
})
example.explanation: This test intercepts the component's HTTP request with MSW and waits for the user-visible heading.

Define a handler for the HTTP method and request path your component calls.
Return a realistic JSON response so the component exercises its normal success path.
Use a dedicated test to verify the UI behavior when the server responds with an error.
Use an asynchronous user-facing query to wait for the response-driven UI update.
gotchas: Reset handlers after each test so an error-specific override does not leak into later tests.
Close the mock server after the suite to release its interception resources.

Async behavior::waitForElementToBeRemove.summary: Wait for an existing element or group of elements to be removed from the DOM. It is useful for asserting that loading or temporary UI has disappeared after an asynchronous operation.
Async behavior::waitForElementToBeRemove.explanation: Pass an existing element or a callback that returns an element or array of elements. The helper observes DOM mutations while waiting for removal and resolves when the target is gone; because the target must exist initially, use a non-throwing query such as queryByText inside a callback when the element may disappear.
Async behavior::waitForElementToBeRemove.syntax: function waitForElementToBeRemoved<T>(callback: (() => T) | T, options?: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }): Promise<void>

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: An element, array of elements, or callback returning an element or array of elements. It must initially identify existing element(s).

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options forwarded to waitFor, including container, timeout, interval, onTimeout, and mutationObserverOptions.

example.title: Wait for a loading message to disappear
example.code:
import {render, screen, waitForElementToBeRemoved} from '@testing-library/react'
import Status from './Status'

test('removes the loading message', async () => {
  render(<Status />)

  await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText('Loading...'))

  expect(screen.getByText('Ready')).toBeInTheDocument()
})
example.explanation: Waits for the initially rendered loading message to leave the DOM, then checks the completed state.

useCases.scenario: A temporary success, error, or status message is removed after an action.

Its behavior builds on the general waitFor utility.
A callback is reevaluated after DOM mutations and completes once the queried target is removed.
Mutation observation avoids regularly polling the DOM for this removal case.
gotchas: The target must exist before waiting; passing null or an empty array fails immediately.
Do not use this helper to wait for something that has not appeared yet.

Interactions::Testing forms.summary: Test forms from the user’s perspective: find accessible fields, enter values, submit through the visible button, and assert the submitted data.
Interactions::Testing forms.explanation: Use accessible role and name queries to locate form controls, interact with them through userEvent, and verify the submitted result. The documented example waits for the submission assertion because the form handler is asynchronous.
Interactions::Testing forms.syntax:
const user = userEvent.setup()
await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', {name: /field name/i}), value)
await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', {name: /submit/i}))
await waitFor(() => expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expectedValues))
Interactions::Testing forms.returns: The test passes when the form submits the expected values to its callback.

example.title: Test a submitted form
example.explanation: Render the form, fill its accessible fields, submit it as a user would, and assert the callback receives the entered values.

useCases.title: Verify successful submission
useCases.scenario: A form accepts valid user input and passes the resulting object to an onSubmit callback.

useCases.title: Handle async submission
useCases.scenario: A form uses asynchronous submission logic before invoking its callback.

useCases.title: Exercise accessible form controls
useCases.scenario: A test should interact with fields using the same labels and controls a user sees.

keyPoints: Create a user with userEvent.setup() and await typing and clicking operations.
Fill each field by querying its textbox role and accessible name.
Submit through the visible button interaction, matching the user's workflow.
Assert the submitted outcome by checking the callback received the expected form values.
gotchas: Wait for the submission assertion when the form's submit handler performs asynchronous work.
Prefer userEvent for realistic interactions rather than directly invoking component internals.

Interactions::userEvent interactions.summary: Use user-event to test realistic browser interactions—typing, clicking, tabbing, and keyboard input—instead of firing isolated DOM events. Create a session with userEvent.setup() and await its interaction methods.
Interactions::userEvent interactions.explanation: user-event APIs describe user interactions rather than isolated DOM events. A setup-created instance maintains input-device state, and its asynchronous methods model browser-like checks and event sequences for actions such as typing, clicking, tabbing, and keyboard input.
Interactions::userEvent interactions.syntax:
const user = userEvent.setup()
await user.click(element)
await user.type(element, text)
await user.keyboard(text)
await user.tab()

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The target element to interact with; required by APIs such as click(), type(), and tab() uses an options object.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text or keyboard-action notation describing input for type() or keyboard().

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration such as skipClick, skipHover, shift, or focusTrap, depending on the API.

Interactions::userEvent interactions.returns: Interaction methods return Promises; for example, click(element: Element): Promise<void> and tab(options: {shift?: boolean}): Promise<void>.

example.title: Model a complete user interaction
example.code:
import {render, screen} from '@testing-library/react'
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event'
import {expect, test} from 'vitest'

function Form() {
  return <>
    <label htmlFor="name">Name</label>
    <input id="name" />
    <button onClick={() => document.body.dataset.sent = 'true'}>Send</button>
  </>
}

test('user can fill and submit the form', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup()
  render(<Form />)
  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Name'), 'Ada')
  await user.tab()
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', {name: 'Send'}))
  expect(document.body.dataset.sent).toBe('true')
})
example.explanation: Creates a user-event session, then models typing, tabbing, and clicking as a real user would perform them.

Interactions::userEvent keyboard flows.summary: Use userEvent.keyboard() to test realistic keyboard sequences, including typing keys, focus movement, shortcuts, modifiers, repetition, and selection-related key behavior.
Interactions::userEvent keyboard flows.explanation: Use a configured user-event instance to model a keyboard flow: move focus with tab(), then send key descriptors with keyboard(). The keyboard API supports printable characters, KeyboardEvent.key descriptors, KeyboardEvent.code descriptors, held keys, repetition, and explicit release. Await each interaction because these APIs return promises.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: A string describing printable characters, KeyboardEvent.key descriptors, or KeyboardEvent.code descriptors and their key transitions.

example.title: Keyboard navigation and shortcuts
example.code:
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react'
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event'
import '@testing-library/jest-dom'
import App from './App'

test('moves through controls with the keyboard', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup()
  render(<App />)

  await user.tab()
  expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Open menu' })).toHaveFocus()

  await user.keyboard('{Enter}')
  expect(screen.getByRole('menu')).toBeVisible()

  await user.keyboard('{Escape}')
  expect(screen.getByRole('menu')).not.toBeVisible()
})
example.explanation: Creates one user-event session, moves focus with Tab, and exercises Enter and Escape as keyboard actions.

Use getByTestId only when the element cannot reasonably be matched by a role or text, such as dynamic or otherwise non-user-visible content; each get query returns one match and throws when none or multiple matches exist.

The getBy family is for finding one matching element.

Queries::within.explanation: Call `within` with a DOM element to receive query functions bound to that element. In React Testing Library, this lets a test identify a repeated or named region first and then search only within that region, avoiding matches elsewhere in the rendered document.

parameters.name: node
parameters.description: The DOM element whose descendants the returned query functions will search.

Queries::within.returns: An object containing query functions bound to the supplied DOM element.

keyPoints: Use `within` when a query should consider only descendants of a specific element.
It returns query functions already scoped to the supplied element, so the container does not need to be passed repeatedly.
React Testing Library uses this scoping approach internally, and the DOM API recommends it for libraries built on the API.
The returned object exposes normal query methods, such as `getByText`, which can be called directly on the scoped result.
`screen` is effectively a collection of queries pre-bound to `document.body`, using the same underlying scoping mechanism.
gotchas: Pass an actual DOM element to `within`; it is an alias for `getQueriesForElement` and binds the raw queries to that element.

Test design::Accessibility assertions.summary: Test UI through semantic roles, accessible names, exposed states, and realistic keyboard interaction. Prefer role queries with name or state filters so component tests reflect how users and accessibility APIs find controls.
Test design::Accessibility assertions.explanation: Use user-facing queries to locate elements by semantic role and accessible name, assert relevant ARIA state, and exercise keyboard interaction with user-event. This keeps normal component tests aligned with browser accessibility APIs and real user behavior.

parameters.description: Optional filters including accessible name, description, hidden status, and ARIA states such as selected, busy, checked, pressed, current, or expanded.

Test design::Avoiding implementation det.summary: Write tests around what users can see and do, not component state, private methods, lifecycle methods, or child-component structure. User-centered DOM queries and assertions make tests more resilient to implementation-only refactors.
Test design::Avoiding implementation det.explanation: Design React tests around the DOM and interactions available to users. Query controls by accessible roles or labels, perform realistic actions, and assert the resulting visible behavior instead of inspecting component internals.
Test design::Avoiding implementation det.syntax: render(ui); screen.getByRole(role, options); screen.getByLabelText(text); userEvent interactions; expect(visibleOutput)

example.title: Test the visible login outcome
example.code:
import {render, screen} from '@testing-library/react'
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event'
import LoginForm from './LoginForm'

test('shows an error when login details are invalid', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup()
  render(<LoginForm />)

  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', {name: /email/i}), 'wrong@example.com')
  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/password/i), 'bad-password')
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', {name: /sign in/i}))

  expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent(/invalid/i)
})
example.explanation: The test interacts through accessible controls and verifies the error visible to the user, without inspecting state, methods, lifecycle hooks, or child components.

keyPoints: Model tests on real user interactions: locate what users can find, operate it as they would, and check the resulting behavior.
Prefer DOM queries that reflect how users find elements instead of selecting component instances or private implementation data.
Keep assertions focused on externally observable behavior so implementation-only refactors are less likely to break the suite.
A refactor that preserves functionality should normally leave these tests intact, because they target the user-facing contract.

Avoid calling component methods directly; verify the behavior produced through the UI.
Lifecycle methods are implementation details and are not user-observable contracts.

Test design::Cleanup and isolation.summary: Call cleanup after each test when automatic teardown is unavailable. It unmounts trees rendered by React Testing Library, preventing leaks and cross-test interference.
Test design::Cleanup and isolation.explanation: React Testing Library tracks trees created by render and cleanup unmounts them after a test. Test frameworks that provide a global afterEach register this automatically; otherwise, connect cleanup to the framework's after-test hook yourself. This prevents leftover DOM and mounted trees from affecting later tests and helps avoid leaks and non-idempotent tests.
Test design::Cleanup and isolation.returns: Unmounts React trees that were mounted with render.

example.title: Clean up after each test
example.code:
import { cleanup, render } from '@testing-library/react'
import test from 'ava'
import { Widget } from './Widget'

test.afterEach(cleanup)

test('renders the widget', () => {
  render(<Widget />)
})
example.explanation: Registers React Testing Library cleanup with AVA so each test unmounts rendered trees and starts with an isolated DOM.

useCases.title: Manual teardown
useCases.scenario: Using a test runner without a global afterEach hook.

useCases.title: DOM isolation
useCases.scenario: Ensuring rendered components do not remain mounted between tests.

useCases.title: Reliable test suites
useCases.scenario: Avoiding memory leaks and non-idempotent tests.

keyPoints: cleanup removes the React trees created by render.
Jest, Mocha, and Jasmine-style environments generally invoke cleanup automatically when they expose afterEach.
For runners without automatic integration, attach cleanup to the runner's per-test teardown hook.
Skipping cleanup can cause memory leaks and allow one test's state or DOM to influence another.
gotchas: If the test framework does not provide automatic cleanup, omitting cleanup after render can leak memory and make tests non-idempotent.
Do not assume cleanup is automatic: explicitly register it when the runner lacks a global afterEach hook.
